speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will have learned with deep regret of the passing, during the Easter recess, of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, Mr. Hugh McKinnon.
Before resuming our sessional duties, I should like to express the sense of loss we experience to-day as we realize he is no longer with us.
Mr. McKinnon was a member of this house for nearly ten years, having been first returned to parliament in a by-election in September, 1934. He was reelected at the general elections in 1935, and again in 1940.
Mr. McKinnon was bom in Kenora, and at the time of his death had all but completed his fifty-ninth year. His interest in. public life first manifested itself in municipal affairs and, later, in provincial affairs. He was, for a time, member of the town council of Kenora, and at the age of forty-one was a candidate for the Ontario legislature. Though unsuccessful in the contest, he lost none of the personal popularity he enjoyed among those who knew him best, and when first nominated as a candidate for the federal parliament he carried the constituency by a majority of over six thousand.
Mr. McKinnon will be remembered by his fellow-Canadians for his deep interest in and practical knowledge of the problems of labour, and of railway labour in particular. He himself had become a locomotive engineer when he was scarcely twenty-one years of age, and his knowledge of our country's political as well as industrial problems was gained in the school of practical experience. He was a devoted member of the Brotherhood of Loco-

The late Hugh B. McKinnon
motive Engineers. There could be no higher testimony to his ability and , fidelity than the regard in which he was held by the entire membership of this enlightened and powerful organization. Recognition of this confidence found expression as early as 1928 in his appointment as one of the technical advisers to the Canadian delegation to the conference of the International Labour Office of the League of Nations, which was held at Geneva that year.
As we in this parliament recall our association with the late Mr. McKinnon, we think of him as one of the kindliest and most modest of men, faithful in his attendance at house sittings, constant in his interest in its proceedings, and deeply solicitous in his own quiet and unassuming way, of the well-being of his fellowmen wherever opportunities to serve their interests arose.
In my last conversation with him in one of the lobbies of this house, he spoke with great earnestness of some of the problems he saw looming on the horizon and of the manner in which he believed they could be most effectively met. I need hardly add that our conversation had to do with the closest possible cooperation of all classes in the prosecution of the war, and in the solution of post-war problems.
Our country and our parliament owe a great debt to men of the type of the late Mr. McKinnon, who look to what is best in human nature, and whose constant effort it is to remove distrust, and to establish confidence wherever that is possible in the affairs of industry and of the state.
I personally feel very deeply the loss of so loyal a supporter and so true a friend as Mr. McKinnon was to me at all times. This sense of loss I know is shared to the full by my colleagues and by all hon. members who sit on this side of the house. I know I can say, wholly irrespective of party political affiliations, that Mr. McKinnon's passing will be felt by all hon. members as a distinct loss to the membership of this house.
Mr. McKinnon is survived by his wife and seven children, four daughter and three sons, two of 'whom, still young in years, are serving in the armed forces, both have been overseas.
I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, to convey to Mrs. McKinnon and to all the members of her family, the expression of the great respect in which her late husband's memory is held by all members of this house, and of the deep sympathy felt by hon. members for her and for all the members of her family in their bereavement.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the friendship of the various men with whom one comes in contact is one of the treasured prizes of public life. Hugh McKinnon was a member of the house whose friendship I was honoured to have. I liked his approachability, his open manner, and regardless of any political divisions in this parliament I am sure he was beloved by all hon. members. He was one of the workers of Canada who had been raised to high positions of honour by those who knew him best. He was in every respect what is known as a self-made man, and for this we in the House of Commons honour him.
As the Prime Minister has pointed out, Hugh McKinnon was a great exponent of the principles and ideals of the Labour movement. He wTas a member of that movement, and the very last time I heard him speak in this chamber was in connection with that beloved topic of his. His words always carried exceptional weight in this house, despite the fact that the opportunity of debate Was not always his, because every member believed that when he spoke he expressed his true convictions.
Mr. McKinnon represented one of the great developing constituencies in Canada, and his friendship particularly for those who worked with him through the years in the railway brotherhood was something which I think all of us would wish to have brought to the attention of the house, as the Prime Minister has done to-day. His only two sons of military age are in the armed forces, and two Sons-in-law have been overseas in this war, so that what the late Hugh McKinnon himself contributed by way of public service to his country is being continued, and the torch carried by his family to-day.
I want to extend to the Prime Minister and to the government on behalf of His Majesty's Loyal Opposition our sympathy in their great loss of a respected and beloved colleague. To Mrs. McKinnon and the family goes out our deep and genuine sympathy, and I should like to be associated with the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker, in the message of sympathy which you have been asked to convey to the bereaved wife and family.

Mr. Speaker, we wish to join in this expression of sympathy for Mrs. McKinnon and the family, and also to associate ourselves with those who have expressed sympathy with the Prime Minister in the loss of a faithful friend and follower. From time to time when we
Mutual Aid-French Agreement

reassemble after an adjournment we are shocked to find that one or more of our membership have passed to the great beyond. Indeed, in the midst of life we are in death, and I think that is brought home to us in this house more directly than in most other spheres of peaceful activity.
Mr. McKinnon, as the Prime Minister has said, was a good member of this house, and a good representative of the calling which he followed. I have heard engineers of the town of Kenora say, when I have been visiting there, that Mr. McKinnon was one of the best engineers who served the great railway system which he joined many years ago. I had the privilege of meeting him on the committees of this house more frequently than perhaps in any other parliamentary activity, and I always appreciated his kindly manner and the sense of responsibility which he displayed under all circumstances. We of this party wish to join in the expression of sympathy which you will convey, Mr. Speaker, to his widow and family.

Mr. Speaker, the words of the Prime Minister and of the two other hon. members who have preceded have pictured a very fine man. I knew Mr. McKinnon personally and have a similar opinion of him, and I desire to join with the Prime Minister and those who have already spoken in words of appreciation of this good man's good life and in words of sympathy to those who are bereaved.

Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to add a word of tribute to the late Hugh McKinnon? It was my privilege four or five years ago to have him at my home in the city of Toronto for a week, at which time he was very much interested in the transportation problem that we had in that centre, and I must say that we enjoyed having him with us. He was a Christian gentleman of the highest order. He had intensely studied the subject in which he was interested, and it was a great pleasure to be associated with him. While he was in Toronto he gave his earnest attention to some of the industrial problems of that great centre, for he had a conception of what the industrial life of the centre of the central province means to his own community.
I have felt keenly the passing of the late Hugh McKinnon, and I desire that it go on record that we thought highly of him, and that we extend to his good wife and the members of his family our sincere condolences. I trust that you, Mr. Speaker, will find a way of embodying these sentiments in the records of the House of Commons.

subtopic: TABLING OF AGREEMENT WITH THE FRENCH COMMITTEE OF NATIONAL LIBERATION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: TABLING OF AGREEMENT WITH THE FRENCH COMMITTEE OF NATIONAL LIBERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to table copies of the mutual aid agreement which was signed on Friday last with the French Committee of National Liberation.
Hon. members will recall that on March 16 I gave a lengthy statement on the mutual aid agreements with the United Kingdom, the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, and Australia. Since that time a similar agreement has been signed with China. The present agreement with the French committee is thus the fifth to be concluded. All agreements are substantially the same in form and are identical in purpose and principle. The present agreement differs from the agreement with the United Kingdom only in a few minor particulars-chiefly matters of terminology- arising out of the fact that the committee has not the formal status of a government.
The agreement which I am tabling sets forth the general terms and conditions under which war supplies are being transferred under the Mutual Aid Act. The fact that no agreement has been signed until now does not, of course, mean that no supplies have yet been sent under the principles of mutual aid. The agreement merely sets out in formal terms the conditions under which such aid has already been sent and under which it will continue to be sent in future. As I pointed out on March 16, there will be an opportunity of discussing the terms of the various agreements when the mutual aid legislation is before the house, and at the moment I wish only to acquaint the house with the fact that this further agreement has been signed, and to make public the terms.
It gave me particular pleasure to sign this agreement, just as it now does to lay it before the house. We have, in the provision of mutual aid, a tangible and most practical demonstration of the cooperation between Canada and the French committee in the prosecution of the war. The committee is carrying forward the great traditions of France in its unrelenting fight against our common enemy, and it will be, I am sure, a source of satisfaction to all the people of Canada that we are able to help in this direct and practical way.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to table three copies of the treaty between Canada and the Republic of China concerning the relinquishment of extraterritorial rights and the regulation of related matters, with exchange of notes, signed at Ottawa on April 14, 1944.
With respect to the treaty which I have just tabled, it is similar in its terms to the British extraterritorial treaty concluded on be-100-130
half of the United Kingdom, Northern Ireland and India on January 11, 1943, and to the United States treaty with China, concluded on the same day.
On the coming into force of the treaty, all international agreements which authorize British or Canadian authorities to exercise jurisdiction in China over Canadian nationals are abrogated. The government of Canada agrees to cooperate w'ith the government of the Republic of China, to the extent that any Canadian interest may be involved, in arrangements for the abandonment by foreign govenments of special privileges hitherto held by them in Peiping, Shanghai, Amoy, Tientsin and Canton.
The relinquishment of extraterritorial rights does not affect existing rights of Canadian nationals with regard to real property in China. It is agreed that Canadian property in China will be subject to Chinese laws concerning taxation and national defence. Real property held by Canadian nationals in China may not be alienated to the government or nationals of a third country without the consent of the government of China. The Chinese government agrees to apply this restriction on alienation in an equitable manner, and undertakes to take over the property in question and pay adequate compensation therefor, if the right to transfer is refused.
Canadian nationals in China are to be accorded the right to travel, reside and carry on trade in China. Each country is to endeavour to accord to nationals of the other, treatment not less favourable than that enjoyed by its own nationals in regard to legal proceedings, the administration of justice and the levying of taxes.
Consular officers of each country may re side in such places as are agreed on. They are to have the right to interview and to communicate with nationals of their country, are to be informed whenever any such nationals are under arrest, and may visit such nationals and receive communications from them.
The treaty provides that, not later than six months after the cessation of hostilities, the two governments will enter into a comprehensive modern treaty of friendship, commerce, navigation and consular rights; meanwhile, questions affecting the rights of Canadian nationals in China and questions affecting the sovereignty of the republic of China, which are not covered by this or previous treaties, will be decided in accordance with generally accepted principles of international law.
Chinese Immigration

This treaty forges yet another bond with our great ally China, which has so long resisted our common enemy. It is evidence, not only of the solidarity of the united nations in the present struggle, but of their determination to preserve the good relations which have been built up during the war and to continue them into a lasting peace.
With regard to the question which the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) asked a few moments ago, I would say that the treaty will 'be brought before parliament for the purposes of approval, and will subsequently be ratified. At the time that the treaty is before the house for approval I shall seek to give my hon. friend the answer to the question he has asked.

subtopic: DRAFT TREATY FOR RECIPROCAL ADMISSION OF NATIONALS FOR TEMPORARY RESIDENCE
speechtext:
My hon.
friend's thoughts and mine are running along the same line.
On January 17, 1944, we presented the Chinese minister with a draft of an immigration treaty, which, if approved and implemented by Canadian legislation, would supersede the Chinese Immigration Act of 1923 against which so many protests have been made.
The draft treaty provides for the admission to either country on renewable permits for temporary residence of nationals of the other country belonging to approved categories (merchants, doctors, ministers of the gospel, et cetera). The treaty is entirely mutual and reciprocal and will, we hope, meet Chinese views without causing opposition in any part of Canada.
The draft treaty has no parallel in any other country. The. United States is meeting the same problem by admitting a small number of Chinese as permanent immigrants under the American quota system.
We are now waiting for a reply from the Chinese government to our proposals.

1.	A subsidy was paid by the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation Limited on
Questions

imported new .potatoes ordered on and after May 3, 1943 -and entered for consumption between, June 3 and 6 pm. July 3, 1943. Potatoes for which forward contracts had been placed prior to July 3, 1943 were eligible for subsidy if entered for 'consumption or shipped on a through bill of lading before midnight, July 8, 1943. Imports up to and including July 31, 1943 were eligible for subsidy only if a permit for the importation had been obtained from the Foods Administration. Subsidy was payable to the importer obtaining title from the supplier in the U.S.A.
The subsidy payable was the amount by which the laid-down cost of the potatoes at the Canadian distribution point to which the potatoes were shipped by the foreign supplier exceeded the wholesale ceiling price for carload lots at that point as set by order 236 of the wartime prices and trade board and its amendments. Applicants were permitted to claim, in addition, a shrinkage allowance equal to 5 per cent of the total value of the potatoes at ceiling prices. Orders on and after June 3, 1943, were ineligible for subsidy if the price per 100 lbs. f.o.b. foreign supplier's shipping point exceeded either (i) the OPA ceiling price plus brokerage and other charges recognized by the OPA, or (ii) $3 (U.S. currency) including brokerage, whichever was the lesser.

I had the privilege of presiding over the conference, which was attended by Hon. Mr. McDiarmid, minister of mines and natural resources of Manitoba, which department is concerned with fisheries matters; Hon. Briefly, the conference decided that for the present attention should be given particularly to whitefish production and marketing, and three major steps were unanimously agreed upon. First, the provinces will make surveys of their whitefish-producing waters, under the guidance of the federal fisheries research board; second, the board will undertake a programme of fresh water fisheries research; third, machinery will be set up, by my department and the provinces jointly, under which all whitefish intended for shipment out of any of these provinces will be subject to inspection.

As for research, I expect in the next few days to be able to announce the appointment of a highly competent chief biologist. The research programme in the provinces thereafter will be developed as quickly as may be efficiently possible. In connection with this, though I do not mean that this particular step can be undertaken at once, we intend to establish in the prairie provinces a permanent fisheries research station, broadly similar to stations such as the research board now operates on the two coasts.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
As I indicated on the eve of the recess, Mr. Chairman, the government is bringing forward the different resolutions appearing on the order paper to-day to enable the bills based upon these resolutions to be brought before hon. members at the earliest moment possible. I hope it will suit the convenience of the house to have the discussion on these matters of social legislation take place on the bills rather than on the resolutions. Unless we agree to that I am afraid a great deal of the time of parliament will be taken up in discussion which will be duplicated when we are on the bills, and this at a time when it is necessary to make as much headway as possible unless the session is to be very greatly prolonged. The

Department of Reconstruction
bills with respect to most of the resolutions have been prepared and could be introduced as soon as the resolutions are carried.
The resolution now before the committee relates to one of three measures mentioned in the speech from the throne, each having to do with the broad field of post-war planning. Hon. members will recall that the speech from the throne mentioned that it was intended to establish the following departments of government:
(1)	A department of veterans' affairs to have charge of the rehabilitation and reestablishment of members of the armed forces, and the administration of veterans' pensions and allowances;
(2)	A department of reconstruction to promote and coordinate planning for national development and post-war employment; and
(3)	A department of social welfare to organize and to assist in administering activities of the federal government in the fields of health and social insurance.
The resolutions on the order paper immediately following the one now before the committee relate to the departments of veteran's affairs and social welfare. If the resolution respecting the department of reconstruction is carried and the bill introduced, the next order will be the resolution relating to the department of veterans' affairs. I do not think it would be advisable to proceed at present with the third resolution, respecting the department of social welfare. We should, I think, wait for the further reports of the special committee on social security, since matters may come from that committee which it might be desirable to have incorporated in the bill. The necessity of establishing a department of reconstruction is, I believe, self-evident. I imagine that there is no difference of view as to that-as between any of the parties in this House of Commons.
As an illustration of the need for this department of government I. might mention briefly two or three essential considerations. The problem of reconstruction will involve the reemployment of nearly two million Canadians now in the armed forces, the merchant navy or war industry. Employment must be productive and must contribute to a rising standard of living. The great industrial plant created for war purposes must be transformed to meet peace time demands in Canada or abroad. Markets must be found and retained for our greatly increased food production unless we are not to face an agricultural depression. Railways, highways and other capital equipment which has suffered the strain of war must be repaired. Civilian aviation and other new means of transport and communication must be developed. Public works and conservation and developmental projects will
be required, particularly while private industries are being converted to peace time operations. New housing, both urban and rural, improvements to existing housing and community planning can contribute at once to the volume of employment and the improvement of the standard of living.
These are merely a few of the directions in which reconstruction planning requires to be carried on. Obviously most, if not all, of these functions relate specifically to some existing department of government. A question naturally arises as to why, if that is so, the planning should not be left to each separate department? It will be, I think, obvious that if the government were to proceed in that way there would be the possibility of much duplication and there would not be the opportunity for the coordination of post-war planning which is essential. Moreover, the problem is so large and at the end of hostilities it will be so urgent, that some special agency is necessary to see that plans are made and action is being taken in all the varied fields in which action will be required if we are to achieve and maintain the full employment and full production which are essential to secure the prosperity and welfare of our people.
The bill which will be based upon this resolution, what it sets forth of the method of proceeding with regard to industrial reconstruction, provides for action similar to that which has been taken in the United Kingdom. There, as hon. members know, Lord Woolton has been selected as minister of reconstruction. Lord Woolton has not a department of government of his own, rather he presides at meetings of his colleagues representing other departments of government. Along with the experts by whom he is surrounded, he meets with these ministers and brings forward plans of reconstruction, obtains information from the different departments of government as to the projects that are already being proceeded with, and makes suggestions as to methods by which existing and other plans can best be furthered and developed.
In Canada, we propose to have, in addition to a minister, a department of reconstruction, in order that there may be, so far as this country is concerned, the necessary machinery of government to effect the coordination that will have to take place, not only between the departments of government at Ottawa but also between the dominion government and the several provincial governments as well as municipalities in the provinces. The intention is to make provision for a minister of reconstruction, a deputy minister, and such staff as may be needed to carry on the work.
Department oj Reconstruction

speechtext:
It will be
necessary to have a parliamentary assistant. I think this is one case where a parliamentary assistant will be of great assistance to the minister and to hon. members of the house. I would say that most certainly there will be a parliamentary assistant.
Perhaps I could indicate, by reading from a section or two of the bill, which will later be introduced if the resolution is carried, the scope of the work for which 1 the minister will be responsible. The interpretation section defines what is meant by "reconstruction," and I shall read that section because it gives the comprehensive picture which I think hon. members will wish to have. It reads:
"Reconstruction" means the reestablishment in civil life and reemployment on demobilization of the men and women of the armed services, reestablishment of persons released from war industries, and the reorganization of industry, in order to provide maximum production and full employment during and following the change over from war time production of industry to peace time production, and includes every undertaking by dominion, provincial or municipal authority or by any corporation or other person which may contribute to such reorganization.
Industry is defined in the following comprehensive terms:
"Industry" includes merchandising, manufacturing, trading, engineering, construction or building operations, the operation of public utilities, transportation and the production of all natural products including the products of farms, forests, mines and fisheries and also any other undertaking by any person including His Majesty in right of Canada or of any province involving the employment of persons during reconstruction.
It is not the intention under this legislation to appoint as minister, for the present at least, anyone from outside the present membership of the cabinet. It is intended that one of the members of the present administration will be appointed minister of reconstruction and will have that responsibility. The reasons for this will be quite clear. It is obvious that the minister who is to be in charge of reconstruction should be a member of the government who is already familiar with the work of the administration. Equally important, he should be one who knows his colleagues intimately, that he will be in a position to confer readily with the ministers of all departments in a manner which will best serve to gain their full cooperation in carrying out the government's policies with respect to reconstruction.
I should like to read what Lord Woolton had to say in the House of Lords in describing his functions. Under the proposed legislation

the Canadian minister of reconstruction will have functions which are very similar. The wisdom of following a similar course will be admitted when hon. members hear what Lord Woolton has said. Speaking in the House of Lords on December 8 last, Lord Woolton gave the following indication of the scope of his functions:
The preparation of plans, the primary responsibility for formulating the plans rests with the ministers in charge of the departments. These plans of reconstruction are not going to be carried out by me. They are going to be carried out by a number of ministers and government departments. The primary _ responsibility for executing them, must continue to rest with the departments concerned, working under the direction of their ministerial chiefs. That is why there is not going to be any ministry of reconstruction. There is going to be no minister of reconstruction with a large staff attached to it. What I have to try to do is to see the reconstruction plan-as a whole, to lay out the various parts which have to be worked out by the departments, to bring the plans of the various departments in relation with one another and to make sure that there are no gaps, no overlapping, no conflict.
The responsibility therefore of the minister of reconstruction is quite clearly defined. It is his business, with his colleagues, to see that all these plans come into one orderly whole and that nothing is left undone by his colleagues that ought in the opinion of the war cabinet to be done.
In our case it will not be the war cabinet, it will be the full cabinet.
In doing so I shall be helped by a very strong committee of the war cabinet.
In the procedure that we intend to follow, the minister will be assisted by a committee of the cabinet which will be formed subsequently. The names of its members are not set forth in the proposed legislation.
I have received the following additional information about Lord Woolton's functions through the Canadian high commissioner in London, with whom I communicated some time ago:
He has, of course, to keep in touch with a numerous body of committees, both governmental and extra-governmental, who are concerned with the problems of reconstruction. He has to be in continual consultation with his colleagues in the government, and to deal with the innumerable private interests involved in anjr far-reaching scheme of national planning. Not the least difficult part of his task is that he must induce the various government departments involved in any one aspect of reconstruction to maintain the same tempo in their planning and execution of reconstruction policies, so that no one part of a given scheme lags behind the other.
In this work, he is assisted by a very small staff of four specialists, in addition to his secretaries and personal assistants.
The staff contemplated for the Department of Reconstruction is a deputy minister, and

Department oj Reconstruction
such other officers, technical assistants, clerks and employees as are necessary for the proper conduct of the business of the department.
I think I have sufficiently indicated the functions of the minister. His powers will extend to the right to institute inquiries, to require return of information, to consult with representatives of producers, industry, science and labour, to establish committees and inaugurate conferences. The minister will also be obliged to submit an annual report to parliament. Provision is also made for the transferring of civil servants from other departments, and equally there is the power to transfer certain branches of departments, if that be thought advisable, to carry out some of the work that may have to be undertaken by the new department.

The New York branch of the Canadian Legion. He deprecated so much attention being paid to the post-war period and to blueprints for postwar reconstruction, when this war is not yet won. He advanced a theory which I have advanced in this chamber on many occasions, and which I reaffirm to-day. The primary and fundamental duty of parliament, the government, and of every one of us is to keep an eye on the ball, and to win the war before we start to revolutionize the world. I hope that hon. members will pause and consider the underlying theory which I am trying to state. As I look over the war fronts and visualize what may take place almost immediately, I say that this nation requires to concentrate its courage, its industry and its every thought upon what is about to happen in the summer of 1944. Anyone who thinks that the war is over is living in a fool's paradise. Anyone who believes that victory is in sight ought to have his head examined. The longest and the hardest pull on the part of the united nations is still ahead, and the people of Canada are being lulled to sleep by too much talk about

post-war rehabilitation and reconstruction. I am all for post-war rehabilitation of the armed forces, but is it not our immediate duty as members of this house, and particularly is it not the duty of the government of the day-I am sure the Prime Minister will agree with this-to insist that the main and fundamental objective of parliament at this time is to concentrate on the winning of the war? I do not mean that we should obliterate from our minds all thoughts about the post-war period; of course we must think about it. But the setting up. of a ministry merely for the purpose of consultation, and without any administrative functions, if I correctly interpret the Prime Minister's statement, is not going to carry us very far. I would ask the Prime Minister to clarify this matter a little more, because, I confess, my mind has been left confused, and I think the mind of the country will be confused, as to just what the functions of this new ministry are to be. It will be established at considerable expense. We are to have a minister and all the paraphernalia and the bureaucracy which go with the minister, and the staff will grow-make no mistake about that. We are to have a parliamentary assistant, another fifth wheel of the coach, and the first thing we know we shall have a huge structure without any administrative functions. I believe the people of Canada are looking for something more than that. It seems to me that the formation of a ministry without administrative functions is premature. I leave that thought with the Prime Minister.

He would discover that somewhere in one or the other will be found a branch of government which could appropriately administer any conceivable reconstruction projects. But it must be equally obvious that to allow departments of government each separately and individually to make plans and carry them out without any form of consultation to effect the coordination of effort, or to prepare plans without first having a general scheme of reconstruction carefully thought out, and accepted, would be to ignore what will be exceedingly important in the period of reconstruction. Perhaps I might indicate the minister's functions by quoting from the clause of the bill which mentions his duties:
4.	The minister shall prepare, formulate and coordinate plans and projects for reconstruction, and, with the authorization of the governor in council, provide for the carrying out thereof.
5.	It shall be the duty of the minister:
(a)	to inform himself fully of the needs for new employment of the men and women in the armed forces and in industry and the opportunities that will be available to meet those needs as men and women are demobilized from the armed forces and as war production declines;
(b)	to coordinate the actions of other departments and agencies of the government of Canada for the purpose of ensuring that the transition from a wartime to a peacetime economy shall be effected as quickly and as smoothly as possible;
(c)	to formulate plans for industrial development and conversion, public works and improvements, housing and community planning, research and the conservation and development of natural resources, and with the authorization of the governor in council, to provide for carrying out such plans;
(d)	to correlate information relating to plans for reconstruction.
I cannot imagine that there will be any difference of view on the part of hon. members. first, as to the wisdom of having as much of the work of reconstruction carried out as may be possible, by departments already established, and second, as to the wisdom of having some agency which will be responsible for the proper co-ordination or integration of all reconstruction work to be carried on, and responsible to this House of Commons for what is being done in that way.
As to my hon. friend's other remark, he is quite right when he says that I feel very strongly, as he does, that all of us must keep our minds concentrated, that we cannot keep them too much, concentrated, on the war and on the necessity of winning the war. Very few people, I believe, appreciate how very heavy is the task that lies ahead before victory is achieved. I would be the last to ask
parliament to consider any measure at this stage if I felt that it was going to have the effect of taking the minds either of members of parliament or of the people away from the war effort as the first of all our national obligations. I realize, however, as hon. members will, that we owe everything to the men who are fighting at the front, and among our obligations one of the greatest, I think, is to give those men, in the fullest measure possible, the assurance that we are thinking of them while they are fighting our battles and that we are making provision for them when they return, which will help to ensure better conditions than they have hitherto known.
Nothing would more discourage the fighting forces of the country than the thought that this parliament did not have them and their future continually in mind. I appreciate the stress which my hon. friend lays upon the importance of not allowing discussions in this parliament even to assume an emphasis, with respect to post-war matters, which would cause anyone to believe that the war is going to be over soon; and that we can take it for granted that there is not a long and arduous road to be traversed before some of these projects can begin to be put into effect. But our duty, as I see it, is not to delay in the endeavour to make our plans as complete as possible, and to get under way whatever measures we can that will help to give that assurance to those who will be seeking above all else steady employment when they return to this country, and as well new employment, not only for those in the armed forces, but for workers in industry who, during the period of war, have lost or been transferred from their former fields of activity and will have to enter upon new occupations once we return to the days of peace.

speechtext:
We must come to an understanding about this proposal. The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) spoke very well about the soldiers and what is to be done for them. But they are not to be fed with words. Soldiers are realists. Once over the Columbia Broadcasting System network I heard a soldier who was returning from somewhere in the South sea islands making this statement: We are not interested at all in what we may have later on after the war; we want to know what the government is ready to do now for us. He was an American speaking to Americans.
We have heard a good deal about a new order. Will the foundations of the new order be the same as those of the old order? That
Department of Reconstruction

is one point. It is impossible to satisfy the minds, the legitimate desires, of those in the army by telling them of future happiness when there is nothing to give them when they come home right now. I shall have a good deal to say about the resolution concerning the new department of pensions. Now, sir, what is the idea of this department? It will not be an administrative department. The minister will be a kind of liaison officer between heads of departments. The Prime Minister said that this minister will be naturally a member of the cabinet who is familiar with his colleagues, who will speak to them about what they should do with regard to so-called reconstruction.
All the members of the cabinet meet in the council room. Why, therefore, should they need a liaison officer? Why should there be a minister acting as a liaison officer when he is on good terms already with all the ministers and may speak to them about reconstruction? I presume all ministers are on speaking terms. Therefore, why should they not speak to each other about their own problems?
My idea of the cabinet is that the ministers meet together to discuss their own problems and that they accept the decision of the majority of themselves. Why should there be a minister who is just a messenger of council, who goes to the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) and says, "My dear colleague, why do you not do so-and-so for. the miners", and then goes to the genial Minister of Fisheries and says, "I have here a problem for you to consider in regard to the fishermen". And then take the farmers. No minister would speak to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) except the liaison minister, who would go to him and say, "My dear Jimmie, I think you should do so-and-so for the farmers; is it not a good thing for you to do for them?" And he will do that on the suggestion of experts, brain-trust men.
Have we not enough plans now? We are submerged by plans that come from every part of the country. There is not a board of trade, not a chamber of commerce, not a municipal council, not an organization or society in this country that is not planning something for reconstruction after the war. Is it possible to apply all these plans? A selection will have to be made and the selection should be made by the ministers in council, not by one man but by all of them together, subject to the majority of themselves. That is my idea of government.
Why should the government delegate its authority to one minister who will be spokesman, to speak to each one of them? That is the destruction of the principle of govern-

ment as it has been established in England, a principle which has functioned so well for so long a time. Of course, we have heralds who speak over the radio. I do not know whether they speak officially, but they speak over the radio and announce policy. They announce policy before we know it in the House of Commons.
My great fear is the fear of bureaucracy. As was said in the Quarterly Review of the university of Toronto by Professor MacGregor Dawson in the spring of 1941-he is a sensible man although he is in the university of Toronto-we are facing a crisis of authority. No one is ready to take responsibility for what is being done. It is the old story of the little boy who breaks the window. You ask him who did it and he says: "It was my little friend." "Who is that little friend?" He says: "He was passing by and he did not do it himself, but the stone was thrown by the neighbour of my little friend." You ask him: "W'ho was that neighbour?" He says he does not know. No one knew. It is like that. No one is responsible for anything. If we are to have new departments let us have departments where the ministers have authority to do something and where they will be responsible to the House of Commons. It is impossible now to get any information. How often have I asked the Prime Minister to give me some information about expenditures in each department? It is no better now than it was before although fine promises were made.
We are here to maintain at all costs the principle of responsible government. We are here to maintain that during war as well as in peace time, and there is no reason why that should not be done. I see my hon. friend the leader of the Canadian Commonwealth Federation across the way, who has visions and a mirage in mind for this country. When he sees someone suffering he says: "Here I am, I shall make you recover. I have a cure for you." When you ask him what that cure is, it is impossible for him to tell you.
The reason why I object to his policy is that he stated not so long ago that he would use the same people in the service that we have now to promote his own policy. I find that they are not good. I find that most of them should be kicked out. I said that to the hon. member for Parry Sound and the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. I said: "The trouble with you, gentlemen, is that you are two great lawyers. The trouble with you is that you consider the matter as expert legal minds. You make such subtle distinctions! The thing for you to do is to buy a pair of lumberman's boots, take a fork and a

Department of Reconstruction
shovel and shovel those people out." That is the way I understand it. What can you do with bad tools? What could the leader of the C.C.F. group or any leader do with the tools that we have now? They come from universi-ities and they have no practical experience. They have those dreams, but they are far from being equal to Plato, the great Greek philosopher, who thought of an ideal state. What most of them do is to have a scheme, or plan, that will give them the opportunity to have two maids instead of one and change their old car for a brand Dew one. It is a scheme they turn to their own advantage because parliament has no control over bureaucracy. That is it.
What is the use of speaking of parliamentary rights and of the supreme control of parliament when we are treated like children? When we come here it is to impose taxation and approve the spending of money. To-day we have a resolution to constitute a new department. After the bill is passed and the department is constituted, the minister will be just as independent of parliament as any one of his colleagues. We shall have no return. We shall have no public accounts. We shall have no information, and when we ask for some information we shall be told it is too expensive to give it. That is it.
I shall tell the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition, as well as the leaders of other groups that it is time to apply the scissors to bureaucracy. It is time to stop. It is time to think of the date when bureaucracy will be reduced at least by one-half and when we shall dispense with all the fine brains produced by the universities. Some years ago I complained of the teachings that were given especially at the university of Toronto by King Gordon and at Queen's university by another gentleman and at McGill university. What happened? Sir Edward Beattie did not say anything to the students at McGill, but he went to Queen's university and gave a calling-down to the students there. I asked him for a copy of his speech. He sent me others but he did not send me that one. Then what happened? It was the ambition of the key men of the C.C.F. to shape the minds of the university students, to shape them like their own. Then what happened? What happened is that business has taken over the control of universities. The young men who are now students in political economy and political science and like subjects are not used any more by private concerns for statistical work or private planning. They are sent here to the government to look after the interests of big finance. I denounce them now for that very purpose. I knew that most of the Canadian
universities are controlled by big finance. If I am told that the chancellor of Toronto university is the venerable Sir William Mulock I reply that it is easy for anyone to look at the board of governors to see that I do not exaggerate in any way when I speak of the role of high finance on the board there; not only on the board but also on the teaching staff and in the formation of students who come out of that university.
Now, sir, it is time to think deeply. We are here as private members, all of us. The members on the treasury benches as well as those on the opposition benches and back benches are here to discuss the problems of the future of this country. We wonder what will happen. Nothing will be decided by fine phrases or by eloquent speeches. We have to come down to facts. We must be realistic. We must realize that the first thing to do for this country is to cut down the dominion civil service to the minimum, to make a selection and then to have the courage to dispense with those who are useless. How is it that some people who do absolutely nothing in their own offices are kept here? They are kept here because the minister knows them and is afraid to receive complaints from those people if they are fired. In my view it will be a benefit to the country to dispense with a few men at the top and some others at the bottom in order to give the country a breathing spell.
Can we continue to institute new boards, new organizations, new departments? How would it be possible for a businessman to pay for all that? Where is the businessman who is not handicapped by taxes? He has to pay for social work; and1 if we have so much social legislation, it is precisely due to the increasing taxation. Before taxation was at such a height it was possible for private charity to do marvellous things. It was possible for private charity to help a large number of people that no government could provide for. With the burden of taxation ever increasing the Canadian people are becoming slaves in their own country. That is why the government is going after social legislation. I am not against the social happiness of the people. I am all for it. I remember the time when I asked the Prime Minister to help me to prepare statistics with regard to hours of work and minimum wages in the various cities of Canada. I did that before Tom Moore ever spoke of it. I did it before the C.C.F. party ever spoke of it in the House of Commons. I think it was in 1928; anyway, it was a long time ago. I did that with the help of the Prime Minister. I was rebuffed by Tom Moore and the trades and labour congress because I was not a labour man. I was not of the type of Dorothy
Department of Reconstruction

Thompson who makes a million dollars a year and belongs to the C.I.O. in the United States, I am not a hypocrite like that. I was doing that for the welfare of my own people.
What help have we had from the other groups in regard to the welfare of Canadian citizens? They are like Moses; they want to lead the Canadian people into the promised land, but the leader of the C.C.F. party must remember that Moses never got there. What is their suggestion in regard to reconstruction? How do they want to reconstruct this country? Should it be done, as Mr. Woodsworth said during the special session of 1939, by conscripting bank accounts? Is it to be done by preventing people from having any profits? In my view the Canadian people should be just as wealthy as they deserve to be. Every citizen should be entitled to a profit, to enable him to live decently. We must have private initiative. A man has a right to what he earns; a man has a right to save money in order that he may enjoy the comforts of life. A labouring man has as much right as a millionaire to the comforts of life, though he may not have so much money with which to get them. Every man must be enabled to bring up his children decently, to live well, to have all the clothing he and his family needs, and to enjoy at least the life of a decent citizen.
I think this department should be called the pigeon-hole department. It is not that I am against social reconstruction or against the welfare of the Canadian people. I see one of my hon. friends laughing; let me tell him that what I say now is what I have been thinking ever since I read his description of our future happiness. It is dangerous to lead people to expect more than it is possible, to give them. That is what creates communism and disrespect for parliamentary institutions. The situation is so bad that the committee to consider the rules of the house, which was presided over by Mr. Speaker and on which were at least two ministers, the Minister of Pensions and National Health and the Minister of Justice, stated that there was general criticism of parliament throughout this country. We have to think of the safeguarding of our national democratic institutions. A faux pas might have the most serious consequences, and before they go farther I hope the members of the cabinet will think seriously not of what I have said but of the facts I have presented. I am tired of playing the role of Cassandra in this house. I hope what I foresee never will come about, but we must visualize the worst and must act in such a way as not to disappoint the men who are fighting with the Canadian army and

who have every right to expect decent treatment from this country when they return, even before the war is over.
If this proposal goes through, someone will be appointed as minister of reconstruction. In that connection I should like to bring a certain matter to the attention of the Prime Minister, and this will conclude the remarks I have to make at the moment. The late Senator Dandurand described himself in the "Parliamentary Guide" as president of a bank, director of an insurance company, and so on. At the present time one of the Prime Minister's colleagues describes himself as director of the Great West Life company. I see no wrong in that as long as the fact is made public that a cabinet minister is a director of a company. Other ministers, however, have resigned their directorships of banks and other companies before entering the cabinet. I wonder which policy is right, to retain a directorship and make that fact public so that all may know it, or to resign that directorship. Then there are ministers who inform us only through British publications as to the directorships they hold. They form a third class. I ask the Prime Minister to tell me what is the policy of the government concerning ministers who are on the boards of banks, insurance companies, and so on.

speechtext:
I was hoping that we might discuss the appointment of the minister and the setting up of the department when we had the bill before us, because I think that would have facilitated the business of the house and would have given us an opportunity of seeing exactly what is contained in the bill and therefore of discussing the matter more intelligently. I am not going to say very much at this stage. While I agree that the war is not yet won and that we must make it our business to provide everything necessary in order to win it, nevertheless I regard it as imperative that at the same time we should lay the foundations of reconstruction as rapidly as possible. Indeed, throughout the war I have held, as I hold to-day, that the preparations for the prosecution of the war and the foundation of the reconstruction period ought to be considered indivisible.
This afternoon the Prime Minister stated the problem in a very few words. He drew to the attention of the house the fact that at some time we shall have to find something like two million jobs for those who to-day are engaged in war industry or who are serving in the various branches of the armed forces. I am quite in agreement that a minister of reconstruction shall be appointed, but I do think we need to do more than appoint a minister. I am not quite clear as to what

Department oj Reconstruction
will be the duties of this minister, nor shall I be clear about it, of course, until I see the bill. However, it does seem to me that it is not the coordination of the work of the established departments that is necessary but rather that we should be sure we comprehend both the resources we have and the possibilities of using them in the post-war period. It is all very well to say, as the hon. member for York-Sunbury did, "Well, we have to win the war. Meantime these other things may wait." The war is not yet won, but I suppose no problem is more in the minds of the young men and women who are in the armed forces than the problem of what is to become of them when the war ends. Yesterday on the train coming to Ottawa I was talking to two or three men who were sitting in the sleeper. I was not paying particular attention to a young man sitting on the opposite side of the aisle, but all of a sudden he chipped in. He heard us talking about the war and the possibilities of the post-war period. He was a young airman and he said, "Like millions of other boys I am thinking of what is going to happen to me when this war ends if I come back again." It is all very well to say that we have td win the war first, but we should make some adequate preparations so that when people are let out of war industry or return from war service they will not have to go in the bread lines and be put on relief or have to take all kinds of unproductive jobs. The people of Canada are expecting this government and this house to take these matters under consideration now and to be thoroughly prepared when the time comes.
No one will ever be able to make the excuse again that Canada cannot provide for her people. No one ever again will be able to say that there is no money to maintain the essentials of life and to provide a reasonable standard of living for everybody in this country. We have demonstrated in this war, even with the type of planning that has been done-it has been rather haphazard

what might be done in a peace-time period. The first task given to the minister of reconstruction should be that of making a thorough survey of all our resources, both human and material, the laying down of some plans to utilize our material and human resources and to absorb the labour of two million people when this war ends. I believe we can do this if we make up our minds that we will lay down, adopt and follow a far-reaching national plan for the conservation and development of the natural resources we have in this country. This does not mean that this
can be done without some attention being given to external problems of trade and so on, but I believe trade problems can be solved by coming to proper types of agreements with those who are willing to trade with us as we are willing to trade with them.

I have just come back from the .west where I spent a few days. After leaving Ottawa and the other centres in this part of Canada and going out on the prairies I could not help noticing some of the farm homes that I saw. I found some conditions appalling. Of course, some are also appalling in some of our cities, but on the prairies I saw unpainted villages and tiny homes on the farms with very little in them. A few days ago I was in the home of a mother whose son had recently been taken prisoner of war. I saw a tidy, clean, humble home with very little in it, and I realized that while that mother had sacrificed a boy, this country had given her very little in the way of human and material comfort as compensation for the loss and anxiety that she has undergone. As I say, I should like to see a thorough survey made of the possibilities of this country, including rural rehabilitation. I notice the hon. member for Essex East looks rather worried or hurt when I say that.

The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) pretty well expressed the psychology that is abroad when he said this afternoon, "Why consider these matters now; why not leave things more or less to work themselves out?" I Suppose we are to leave things to so-called private enterprise. May I say again that in my opinion along those lines lies disaster. I have on my desk a quotation from a statement made by one of the great students of social and economic relationships. On May 24, 1943, Sir William Beveridge was interviewed in this city by one of the local newspapers and, on
Department oj Reconstruction

being asked whether he thought private enterprise could cope with the post-war problems, made this statement:
I am not at all sure that private enterprise can take the responsibility of both maintaining enterprise and showing a profit. It seems to me difficult, perhaps impossible, thus to serve two masters. I doubt if employment can be maintained without a very considerable proportion of public monopoly in the national economy.
He was then asked, "Don't you think private enterprise should be given a chance?" and he replied:
No, I don't. Not if it can't do the job. I want to take no chances on the maintenance of employment-it's far too important a matter. I would not entrust it blindly to private enterprise any more than private enterprise should be trusted to run a war.
I fear that that is what we are inclined to do as a country, to leave too much to what sometimes is called private enterprise. _
As I said, I did not rise to enter into a prolonged debate on the setting up of this department. I think it should be done, but from what I have heard this afternoon I do not think the functions of the department are sufficiently wide. I do not think they are sufficiently comprehensive. The hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) has referred to bureaucracy. I dislike bureaucracy and I believe that in the future we shall have to devise ways and means of making democracy work. Let me add that we have never been under a greater bureaucracy than the bureaucracy of big business, of private monopoly and of international cartels.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am going to support the resolution. In my opinion, next to the national defence departments, of which there are three, the munitions department and the finance department, the proposed reconstruction department will be the most important. I am one of those who firmly believe that next to the prosecution of the war the preparation for peace is the most important. In supporting any plans for the preparation for peace I do not intend for one moment to

neglect anything I can do to prosecute the war. For the last three years I have been advocating the doctrine of war first and the preparation for reconstruction second.
I believe, further, that this resolution is in line with what was sent from the reconstruction committee which was headed by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Turgeon), who made an excellent chairman. I am sure that he and the other members of the committee, including myself, have done our best to search out from among the proposals that came before us those that would be the most effective in providing employment after the war. I cannot for a minute see why this department should not have been set up some time ago, as the reconstruction committee recommended a year ago, or at least during last session.
I remember very well what happened in 1918. I was in big business then. I quite agree that no one can say that the war is going to end this year, but on the other hand no one can say that it may not end this year. It may end as suddenly as it did in 1918, and suppose it did end this fall, are we ready? We certainly are not. We certainly have not anything ready that I know of, and if this new department can have something in shape and ready it will have done a good job. We should have many projects ready to send thousands and thousands of men to work upon as soon as the war ends, to provide employment while industry is retooling.
I know something about industry; I ought to. I do not for one minute endorse what the hon. member who has just sat down has said about industry. I am going to discuss that for a moment because I am getting tired of listening to that kind of talk. Anyone who has served in big industry for years should know something about it. The man who has not can have his own opinion, but his opinion does not influence mine one iota. Canada owes a great deal to big industry, for the honesty of purpose of big industry and for what it has done for this country. If industry had not given employment to hundreds of thousands of men and women before the war and during the war I should like to know what would have happened to the prosecution of the war. Neither will I endorse what my hon. friend said about private enterprise. I am in favour of private enterprise. I have seen too much waste and too much excessive costs through government conducting business that should have been conducted by private enterprise. But that is not what I rose to say.
People all over this country have been confused over where to send their recommendations on reconstruction, and perhaps the bill

Department oj Reconstruction
to be founded on this resolution will settle some of this confusion that I have found everywhere across Canada, and I have been over most of it. Boards of trade and municipal councils have asked me to whom they should send their reconstruction recommendations. They say that we have three or four committees working on reconstruction, the cabinet committee, the Doctor James committee, the Senate committee and the House of Commons committee on rehabilitation and reconstruction. If this new department will mean the concentration of recommendations and representations before one body, well and good. That will be better than it is to-day, and in saying that I am not casting reflections on any of the committees that have been set up.
Someone has said something about blueprints and specifications. There have to be blueprints and specifications; and if the new minister, whoever he may be, and this new department that is to be set up will take some little advice from the humble member for Davenport they will make many blueprints and many specifications, go into many details and have their plans and projects ready. I could give them a hundred projects myself, every one which is absolutely necessary and for which blueprints and details could and should be prepared now, so that the projects will be ready to start when the war ends. The blueprints and specifications could in the meantime be pigeon-holed after all the details have been worked out, so that when the war ends all that it would be necessary to do in order ta have this or that project started would be to call for tenders and get the men on the job. It would not be necessary to order production of the material in advance, for it would have to be ordered some time; and if everything is in readiness when the war ends, the new department could announce at once that so many million brick would be required for this project, so many thousands of tons of steel for that project, so many million feet of timber for the other project, and so on all down the line. I endorse the proposal, and if the department has not the necessary authority-and the hon. member for York-Sunbury seemed to doubt that it had the necessary authority-I hope that before the bill passes the house the Prime Minister will see to it that the department is given absolute authority to make all preparations necessary for providing men and women with jobs following the war.
I believe there will be about two million jobs required; if you do not make preparations, exactly the same thing may happen that happened after the last war, and there is not
a man or woman in this house who wants to see that occur again. When I say that, I am not blaming any previous government because they had no experience in after-the-war matters. But now we have had the experience of not being ready, and this government has seen what happened through not being ready. I endorse this attempt to get ready, so that when the men return from overseas there will be jobs for them, and jobs in the meantime for men who have already returned and for men who are thrown out of employment from industry. Some days ago I was in an industrial plant which employs several thousands of men and women. Ordinarily, that plant would not run twenty-four hours after the war is over, for the very good reason that it is making things that are wholly needed for the prosecution of the war. I know that some people say: Oh, you will have to keep these plants running, producing munitions and guns that probably will not be needed again for one hundred years, and the guns will be obsolete by that time. That, to me, is not sound economies. I would rather see this new department prepare to do something for Canada, by making plans and preparations for projects all over this country where men and women can be put to work. Many of these projects will be self-liquidating, and a great many of them should have been started years and years ago, projects which in the long run will not cost the country a dollar. When the department is set up I shall be glad to send it lists of projects which I have surveyed myself here and there across this dominion, because I am absolutely sincere in believing that all preparations should be made ahead of time and everything be ready when the war ends. Of course, it will be some time before the soldiers start to return after the war, but many of them have already returned. The hon. member for Temiscouata mentioned, and I had intended mentioning it myself, that many of those who have returned are not working, and if this new department can provide them with jobs and provide with jobs those who are let out from industry, that will be a start. What preparations are made for them? Every day men and women are being released from industries throughout this country. Where are they to be sent? The department should make plans to provide employment not only for those who are returning from overseas but for the great number who are engaged in making munitions of war.
I should like to ask a few questions. When the bill comes down I shall have much more to say. As I understood the Prime Minister, he intimated, although he may not have used these words, that there would be an effort by this department to invite new lines of
Department of Reconstruction

industry. Certainly a vast number should be introduced, for there is much opportunity for them in Canada. Perhaps this department will enable many industrial organizations now established on the other side of the water, and with a number of which I am acquainted, to set up their activities here for this market. I believe that, operating with the consent and assistance of other government bodies, this new department will find here a wide field of usefulness. Some person or some committee having the authority could make a survey of, say, a thousand and one new lines of industry for this country, many of which, if the proper surveys are made beforehand, could be installed in munition plants which, being single purpose plants, will likely close when the war ends, and for which, otherwise, no use might be found. If that is to be part of the work of the new ministry it will have my heartiest support. I am sure that thereby much employment will be provided.
I should like to know also whether this new reconstruction department will be empowered to dig into and set on foot the St. Lawrence deep waterways power project. If that programme, which is known to almost every hon. member as well as to most engineers, were comprised in the activities of the new department, there would be fifty thousand jobs to begin with. Further, the electricity produced by the deep waterway on the St. Lawrence river would provide hundreds of thousands of jobs in new industries. The international section of the St. Lawrence deep waterways alone can generate an additional million cheap horse-power for Ontario, and the Quebec section would allow for the production of another three million horse-power, apart from what will be produced in the United States. This means great numbers of additional jobs.
In my opinion the new department will have to be ready when the war ends to furnish employment for hundreds of thousands of people. I do not believe that the men who come back from this war will tolerate what their fathers had to put up with following the last war, and nobody in this chamber would want them to do so.
I should like to know whether the new department will have any power to associate itself with the vast transportation project which has received the endorsation of engineers and economists, namely the construction of the St. Lawrence deep waterways, which would open up a vast transportation route all the way from Fort William to the strait of Belle isle, a distance of two thousand miles, and, according to the best authorities, would add from three and one-half to five
rMr. MacNicol.]
cents to the value of every bushel of wheat produced in the west. We all know that anything which improves the lot of the western wheat grower will increase purchasing power throughout this country and provide thousands of jobs in industry. Will the new department have anything to do with the construction of the great lakes-St. Lawrence seaway?
One other question. Will the department have anything to do with the programme which, though I make not the slightest claim to its initiation, I strongly supported on February 3, of a giant irrigation project in the west? This would mean directly or indirectly the provision of another hundred thousand jobs. Will the department have anything to do with providing water for the cities of the plains? I have here numerous clippings from western papers in reference to the situation of some cities-Moose Jaw, for one-in respect of water supply. Will the new department be able to initiate a programme of damming the South Saskatchewan river, irrigating the land between Riverhurst and Regina, and providing water in abundance for Regina and Moose Jaw? I am not finding any fault with Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, which has done a fine job. This is not the time to digress and deal with its work, but on an appropriate occasion I shall compliment P.F.R.A. for the work it has done in the matter of dug-outs and small irrigation projects. This new department should be enabled to tell the P.F.R.A. administration to "go ahead and construct the ten thousand projects they have surveyed and approved but which they cannot carry out for lack of money." There, again, would be thousands of jobs. Will the new department be permitted to throw its weight behind projects to rehabilitate the west by providing water where water should be provided? If so, there is another important programme in which it can engage.
I shall not take up the time of the committee to mention other projects, though when the bill comes down I may have more to say along that line. I agree with the Prime Minister that all the work cannot be done in one year or in two years. A large programme must be laid out, perhaps for a period of ten years, and provision must be made for men who will need positions during the after-the-war interim. It will be remembered that after the last war, when the factories were retooled and had caught up with the demand for consumer goods, another big depression came.
If the Prime Minister and the government have the vision which I have of what a department like this can do there will not be an unemployed man or woman in Canada.

Department of Reconstruction
Employment will be available for everybody at good wages. Contracts could be let to provide everybody with jobs. There should not be an unemployed man or woman in a country like ours, filled to overflowing with resources. No country in the world has the resources which Canada has, but access is denied to many of them because of lack of transportation. I believe the Prime Minister mentioned roads. There is room for vast development in that direction. Will the new department have to do with providing the facilities by which these vast resources can be reached?
Further, what cooperation will it have with the provincial governments and the municipal authorities? Apart from the very large projects which will be purely federal government business, will ordinary works be constructed by the provincial governments and the municipalities under the direction of the new ministry? Will the ordinary works, municipal and provincial, be constructed by the municipalities and the provincial governments under the direction of the new ministry, or what will be the association of the new ministry with the provincial governments and the municipalities? I presume it would not really have any association with the municipalities but it could at once do something of vital importance. It could advise the provincial governments and, through them, the municipalities how much money they can have.
If the chairman of the reconstruction committee says a word, as he may, he will tell the committee what I will tell it now, that delegations that came before the house reconstruction committee asked this question:	How
much money are we going to be allowed, and where is the money coming from?
I would like to have the Prime Minister amplify his remarks in that regard. Where is the money to come from? What is the programme for providing the money, or advising the provinces and the municipalities as to how much money they can have? We all read daily of the various provinces setting up reconstruction committees and some have already gone so far as to say that they will put the matter under a minister. They will, therefore, wish to know immediately the programme in reference to finances for the provincial reconstruction departments.
I feel that if the government is sincere-and I have no reason to suggest that it is not; I should not like to suggest such a thing-then, next to the prosecution of the war, we have here the biggest thing it can do, namely, to make preparations to provide employment for the glorious sons of Canada who have demonstrated on fields throughout the world that no soldiers anywhere can surpass them in valour, 100-132
or all equal them. That is about all I have to say. When the bill comes before us I shall go farther in reference to some of these items, but in the meantime I should like to have answers to some of these questions.
